title: Water at the pump
hook: water on one hand, the word spelled into the other, and Helen Keller's locked world opens (The Story of My Life, 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Frankl, and the men who gave away their bread. Your line was my attitude. Which word did you meet the day with? Today, a well house, and one word that opened a world. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

A broken doll lies on the floor by the hearth. The girl who smashed it feels nothing about it, she later writes: no sorrow, no regret. She can't see and she can't hear, and her teacher has been spelling words into her hand day after day, letters pressed into the palm with quick fingers. The girl can copy the shapes. She has no idea they mean anything. So her teacher takes her by the hand, out into the warm day, down the path to the well house, where someone is drawing water at the pump. Today: water at the pump.
screen: `A BROKEN DOLL BY THE HEARTH.` → `LETTERS PRESSED INTO A PALM.` → `DOWN THE PATH TO THE PUMP.`

segments.voice: First, the two hands. This is Helen Keller's own account, in chapter four of The Story of My Life. Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, puts one of Helen's hands under the spout. Cool water rushes over it. Into the other hand she spells w-a-t-e-r, slowly at first, then fast. Helen stands still, all her attention on those moving fingers. Second, the opening. Something like a forgotten memory stirs, she writes, and the mystery of language comes open. In her words: "I knew then that 'w-a-t-e-r' meant the wonderful cool something that was flowing over my hand." Not a shape in the palm. A name for a thing. And if this had a name, everything did. Third, the doll. On the way back to the house, she writes, every object she touched seemed to be alive. She remembers the doll she broke. She feels her way to the hearth, picks up the pieces, and tries, uselessly, to put them together. And now, she says, her eyes filled with tears. She understood what she had done, and she was sorry. A word for water, and then a word for wrong. Fourth, why it's here, in a block on suffering. Her account doesn't say the dark and the silence went away. They didn't. What changed was that she was no longer alone inside them. Someone had reached in with a name, and a word became a bridge between two people. In her book she calls it a living word, one that set her soul free. Not a cure. A way through.
screen: `WATER ON ONE HAND, A WORD IN THE OTHER.` · `THE MYSTERY OF LANGUAGE OPENS.` · `BACK TO THE BROKEN DOLL.` · `NOT A CURE. A WAY THROUGH.` · then, large: `WATER.`

segments.voice: If you have water near you, a glass, a sink, a bottle, let it touch your hand: a few drops on the palm, or your fingers around the cold glass. If you don't, remember the last time water ran over your hands. Close your eyes if you like. Feel only that: cool, wet, moving or still. Then, slowly, trace the letters of the word with a finger of the other hand on your palm: w, a, t, e, r. Feel the thing and its name meet. Let the rest of the room go quiet around it. The bell holds the time.
Helen Keller, blind and deaf, who felt water poured over one hand while her teacher spelled its name into the other, and the world opened. Today's word.
Your line: water. Today, the next time water touches your hands, at a sink or in the rain, stop for one breath, feel it, and name it. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Readers come back to Helen Keller's account of the well house when they think about language, teaching and breakthrough, and the scene is retold in schools and on stage.

Confirm.
Claims rule: Helen's age and the date are left out. 'Day after day' is a soft summary of the teaching before the pump; confirm.
